rules.K1: example: the statement is a fenced code block
rules.K2: non-normative: the section or an enclosing section is front matter, a change log (title 'Changes from ...') or titled *(non-normative)* / *(deferred)*
rules.K3: non-normative: the sentence starts with *(non-normative...)* or *(deferred...)*, or follows such a sentence in the same paragraph; uncertain if it contains an RFC 2119 keyword
rules.K4: requirement: contains an upper-case RFC 2119 keyword (MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL, REQUIRED, ...)
rules.K5: definition: introduces a defined term (bold) or a rule label of its clause
rules.K6: example: starts with e.g. / For example / Example, contains e.g., or lies in an examples section
rules.K7: requirement: lower-case normative word (must, must not, cannot, shall, may only, may not, never)
rules.K8: requirement: a declarative verb from the fixed list (is, are, returns, rejects, traps, ...)
rules.K9: requirement: a table row (normative table: instruction, default, error-code rows state their content in columns, not sentences)
rules.K10: uncertain: none of the above (verbless fragment, list-item fragment)
rules.K11: sub-statement classified K10 inherits the kind of its enumerating sentence

statements.text: **Verifying executor**: an executor that can decide exactly whether a set of wires is clean on every basis configuration (a state-vector or branch-enumeration simulator); every other executor (hardware) is **non-verifying**.
Rules that depend on the difference say which applies (§3.3 `qreg.free`, §10, §17 item 14).

**Effective control context** at a point: the set of wires on the active predicate stack plus the inherited control context (the control wires of every enclosing `ctl` and predicate stack of every enclosing invocation, transitively); duplicates count once.
Its size is the **effective control count**.

```
  CC ──calls──▶ R functions (call/uncall)       CC ──calls──▶ Q regions
  R  ──calls──▶ R functions, Q regions          Q  ──calls──▶ Q regions (§5.5); oracle bodies call lprocs
```
CC runs on the device's classical-control processor; the host reaches the device only through §10.
**No instruction in any tier makes a control or scheduling decision that depends on the value of a wire** except through predication (§3.5).
Gate angles are finite `f64` literals or classical arguments fixed at region entry.
**Call-tier policy** (suite F). The diagram, completed with same-tier calls; a call, uncall or region call outside this table is ill-formed:
CC function | CC and R functions | of a CC or R callee | oracles, actions | –
R function | R functions | of an R callee | oracles, actions | –
oracle body, lproc | – | – | – | `lift.call` of lprocs; `lift.oracle_call`/`lift.oracle_uncall` of oracles; `lift.perm_call` of permutation actions
action | – | – | oracles, actions (§5.3, §5.5) | –
An R function never calls a CC function: CC code may measure and make host requests (§4.1), which an R history cannot reverse.
classical environment | CC, R | dynamic SSA instances (§7.4), block parameters, activation stack, **quantum-register handles** (`qreg[n]`, `qreg[*]`, §3.3), tokens (§5.4)
register and token ledgers | CC, R | every register's id, class, width and state (§3.3); every device-minted token's tuple and validity (§5.4)
classical memory | CC, R | byte-addressed, little-endian, sparse; allocation table (§7.1)
effect tape, entropy tape | R | §7.3
run history | CC, R | one frame per executed instruction (§7.4)
wire store | Q (CC and R via `qreg`) | live wires with roles `input target fault borrowed mutable workspace location cell`
quantum memory | Q | regions of `wire[W]` cells: local (§4.6) or interface (§5.1)
register file | Q | locations of the active oracle and its lproc closure (§3.7)
predicate stack | Q | wires; the active predicate is their conjunction
oracle step state | Q | `pc, pc' : wire[P]`; `faulted : wire`; `code : wire[F]`; `result_val : wire[T]`; counters (§3.7); B frames
budget | Q | classical: B, heap_limit, stack_limit, depth_limit

```
  iN (1 ≤ N ≤ 128)   ptr (width ptr_width)   f64   token   qreg[n]   qreg[*]   region[A,W]
  wire   wire[N]      linear values in structured code and interfaces
  reg[N]              a location (oracle bodies, lprocs); not linear
```
**Widths.** The bound 1 ≤ N ≤ 128 applies to the type `iN` only (a lifted row's `.iN` suffix names a location width, §4.2).

`wire[N]`, `reg[N]` and `qreg[n]` have N, n ≥ 1 and `region[A,W]` has A ≥ 0, W ≥ 1, with no upper bound (a `qreg[*]` register's width is a run-time value n ≥ 0, §3.3 below); a value of these types is a bit-vector of its width in every semantics (§14.1), including interface bundles, pseudo-locations, locations, cells, stack cells and frame slots.

**Linear SSA with implicit versioning** (structured code and CC region calls): a `wire`/`wire[N]` value is produced once and consumed once; mode `in` consumes and re-produces a successor of the same name; `consume` consumes; `produce` creates; a name is not used after `consume`.
**Regions are threaded the same way.** **Indexed operand** `w[i]` (literal i) borrows wire i for one instruction.

**Disjointness.** The wire operands of one instruction are pairwise distinct; **every wire of the effective control context is distinct from every target and from every consumed or produced operand** of an instruction executed under it (so `qpred p; x p` is ill-formed); a predicate wire is not modified between its push and its matching pop; a `qif`/`qloop … while` selector is not modified inside its arms or body.
A region's interface bundles and regions are pairwise disjoint.

**Per-opcode operand schema** (§4.8): every opcode has a tier set, a fixed arity, operand kinds and a result type; results are written first (`w = op a b`), modes are never written, and **result types that are not determined by the operands are written as a suffix** (`r = const.i32 5`, `r = zext.i64 a`, `r = trunc.i8 a`, `r = ptrtoint.i64 p`, `p = inttoptr a`).

Width rules: `binop`/`icmp` operands equal width; `select` arms equal width; `zext`/`sext` strictly widen, `trunc` strictly narrows; `load.iN` and `lift.load.iN` require N ∈ {8, 16, …, 128}; `measure` of `qreg[n]` with n ≤ 128 yields `in`, and `measure.iN` (1 ≤ N ≤ 128) of a `qreg[*]` yields `iN`; signed division truncates toward zero.

The literal c of `const.iN c` and `lift.const.iN c` satisfies −2^(N−1) ≤ c < 2^N and denotes c mod 2^N (both the signed and the unsigned spelling of every value are accepted); any other literal is ill-formed (suite F).

**Lifted width rules** (suite F; a mismatch is ill-formed, never a truncation or an extension). Every address operand (`a` of `lift.load`/ `lift.store`, `p` of `lift.boundscheck`/`lift.free`) and every address result (`w` of `lift.addr`/`lift.alloc`) is `reg[ptr_width]`; the length `n` of `lift.alloc`/`lift.boundscheck` is a location of any width or a literal in [0, 2^ptr_width); `inrange` and every prospective sum are computed at width max(widths of the operands involved) + 1 with no wrap.
The destination of `lift.label` and the operand of `qjumpr` have any width N with 2^N > n (the index-space size).

`lift.call` location arguments have exactly the callee's parameter widths and its destination the callee's result width; its token, classical and region lists match the callee's corresponding groups in count, order and type (§3.7); `lift.ret v` has the containing lproc's result width; `lift.oracle_call`/`lift.oracle_uncall`/`lift.perm_call` operands have exactly the callee signature widths, and `mem` operands name caller regions whose `[A,W]` equal the callee's and whose role is `in` for an `in` slot (an `in` region is never passed to a `mut` slot); `fault C` and `lift.faultif p C` require the literal C < 2^F, where F is the fault width of the containing oracle or, in an lproc, of every oracle whose lproc closure contains it (checked at load and again at link; an lproc in no oracle's closure is checked when linked into one); the width rules above for `binop`, `icmp`, `select`, `zext`, `sext`, `trunc` apply verbatim to their `lift.*` counterparts; the destinations of one `lift.parmov` are pairwise distinct.

**Quantum registers in CC and R.** A **register** is n device-resident wires of one class with a nonzero 64-bit **id**, recorded in the program's **register ledger** with its class, width and state: **live**, **viewed** (one slice of it is live) or **consumed**.
`qreg[n]` is the type of a register whose width n is fixed statically; `qreg[*]` the type of a register whose width is known only at run time (an unsigned 64-bit n ≥ 0).

A `qreg[n]` value may be used wherever a `qreg[*]` is expected; a `qreg[*]` value bound to a `qreg[n]` parameter or block parameter (`call`, `br`, `ret`, launch) or to a slot of width n (region call, §4.7) is checked at that transfer: its width MUST equal the required one.
The `qreg.*` instructions execute in CC and R; `measure` only in CC.

statements.text: An instruction whose precondition fails is a CC trap / R fault (§4.9) with code `FAULT_UB_TRAP` unless the table says otherwise, and has no effect.
An id's value is chosen by the executor (the suites compare ids only for equality); an id is never reassigned to another register while the program is loaded.
**Handle transitions:**

`q = qreg.new cls n` | `n` a literal n ≥ 1 (q: `qreg[n]`) or an `i64` value read unsigned, 0 included (q: `qreg[*]`); the device can provide n wires of class `cls`, else code `FAULT_BUDGET_HEAP` | q live, clean, with a fresh id
`qreg.free q` | q live, not a view, clean on every basis configuration (a verifying executor checks it; on failure q stays live and unchanged; a non-verifying one: §17 item 14) | q consumed

`q2 = qreg.slice q lo len` | q live, not a view; `lo` and `len` each a literal (`len` ≥ 1) or an `i64` value, both unsigned; lo + len ≤ n, computed without wrap (a trap even when literals make the failure evident) | q2 a view of wires [lo, lo+len) of q, of type `qreg[len]` for a literal len and `qreg[*]` otherwise; q viewed; q2 MUST be the operand of exactly one region call and of nothing else; after that call q2 is consumed and q is live again; a use of q while it is viewed traps (the static rule below covers the cases suite F rejects).
Reversing that region call (§7.4) restores q viewed and q2 live; reversing the slice frame then restores q live

`q = qreg.concat q1 q2` | q1, q2 live, not views, distinct registers | q1, q2 consumed; q live, with a fresh id, over the wires of q1 then q2; `qreg[n1+n2]` if both operands are static, else `qreg[*]`
`w = qreg.width q` | q live, not a view | w: `i64`, the width; no state change
`id = qreg.id q` | q live, not a view | id: `i64`, the bits of q's id; no state change

`q = qreg.from_id id` | `id` is the id of a register of the program that is live, not a view, and not owned by another run that is not CLOSED (§10) | q: `qreg[*]`, an alias of that register; no ledger state change; the run now owns the register (§10), which reversal does not undo (ownership ends when the run is CLOSED)
region call (§4.7) with q as operand | q live (a view included); its width equals the slot's (§3.3 binding) | q unchanged

`r = measure q` / `r = measure.iN q` | q live, not a view; the form `measure.iN` (1 ≤ N ≤ 128) for a `qreg[*]`, whose width MUST be N (checked before measuring); for a `qreg[n]` either `measure` or `measure.iN` with N = n (checked statically) | q consumed, its wires released; r: `in` / `iN`
reversal of a `qreg.*` frame (§7.4, §10) | – | the ledger state before that frame (below).
A `measure` frame is **never reversed**: a segment containing one cannot be uncalled (§7.4) and a run containing one is not reversible (§10)

**Ledger frames and their reversal** (§7.4). A `qreg.new` frame records the id, class and width; its reversal releases that register without a test: every later frame touching it has been undone first (LIFO) and the run owns it exclusively (§10), so under T4's exactness hypothesis it is clean, and otherwise its residual, within the declared bounds of the undone realisations (§12.3), is discarded with it.

A `qreg.free` frame records the id, class, width and whether its cleanliness was verified; its reversal re-creates the register clean and live with the same id, class and width (every alias sees it live again).

A `qreg.slice` frame records the parent id, lo and len, a `qreg.concat` frame the two operand ids and the new id; their reversal restores the exact prior states and wire order without moving, copying or measuring a wire.
`qreg.width`, `qreg.id` and `qreg.from_id` change no ledger state and their frames are pure (§7.4); if an `uncall` later removes the register an alias refers to, every use of the alias traps.

**Binding**: a register of width n (`qreg[n]`, or `qreg[*]` of run-time width n) fills a `wire[n]` slot bit for bit (bit 0 ↔ wire 0); it fills a `region[A,W]` slot iff n = 2^A·W with cell i = bits [iW, (i+1)W); for a `qreg[*]` the width is checked at the call, before any effect.
Host-supplied register ids are `qreg` values of the parameter's type.
**Registers, handles and aliases.** A `qreg` value is a reference to a register of the device; the state live / viewed / consumed belongs to the register, not to a name.

`qreg` values pass unchanged as `call` arguments, `ret` values and `br` block arguments (each transfer binds another name to the same register and changes no state; a `qreg[*]` reaching a `qreg[n]` parameter is width-checked, above).
Two names bound to one register (by such transfers or by `qreg.from_id`) are **aliases**: a transition made through either is observed through both.
The wire operands of one region call, with its effective control context, MUST denote pairwise disjoint wires (§3.3 disjointness); aliases violate it.

**Static and run-time verdicts.** Suite F rejects exactly: two `qreg` operands of one region call or of one `qreg.concat` that are the same name; and, on some path from a `qreg.slice`, a use of the view's name other than as the operand of one region call (a `br`, `call` or `ret` transfer included), its reaching a `ret` or the end of the function unconsumed, or a use of the slice's parent operand name before that call.
Every other overlap, and every use of a viewed register through another name, is a CC trap / R fault with code `FAULT_UB_TRAP` before any effect.
Sequential small-step execution with an instruction pointer, block parameters instead of phi nodes, dynamic control flow and allocation; every executed instruction pushes a run-history frame (§7.4).

**Names and definitions.** Every name used in a CC or R function is a parameter, a block parameter or the result of at least one defining instruction of that function, and all its definitions give it one type (suite F).
The text order of blocks is irrelevant: a definition need not precede its uses textually.
Executing a use of a name that has no current instance (none was created on the executed path, or an `uncall` removed it, §7.4) is a CC trap / R fault `FAULT_UB_TRAP`.
Every CC or R block ends in `br`, `ret`, `trap` or `fault` (suite F); `trap` and `fault` end the run (§4.9).
Every Q instruction with unitary semantics executes controlled on the active predicate.
`qpred w` pushes, `qunpred w` pops the same wire; the stack is empty at region entry and exit.
Allocation, borrowing, release, region creation and image gates are **unconditional**; only gates (including those inside copy/XOR/exchange/memory instructions) are controlled.

**Index space.** `I[0..n)` = the **rows** (one index per instruction line) of the oracle's blocks, blocks in text order and rows in text order within each block; then the rows of every lproc in its **lproc closure** (transitively reachable through `lift.call`, linked ones included), placed as follows: partition the closure into its SCCs (§9.2); a one-member SCC's **order key** is its member's closure hash, a multi-member SCC's order key is its closure `scc_hash`; SCCs are placed in increasing bytewise order of their keys (64-hex), the members of a multi-member SCC consecutively in SCC index order; each lproc's binding instances (§3.7) consecutively in binding-key order, each instance's rows in block text order as for the oracle.
The oracle and each lproc instance therefore occupy a contiguous range of indices, and a **label `^b` denotes the index of the first row of block b**.
`HALT = n`; 2^P > n.

statements.text: Branch and call targets are labels; `w = lift.label ^b` is the only way a location obtains an index value; executors MAY re-index dispatch extensionally **provided every label value observable through `lift.label` keeps its canonical numeric value and a `qjumpr` to any in-range index reaches the row that canonical index names**.
**Terminators**: `qjump qbranch qjumpr lift. ret lift.retval fault`; every block ends in one; no label names HALT; **only `lift.retval` reaches HALT with success**.

**Row classes.** Each §4.2 row is an **assignment** (A: written locations/cells receive values computed out of place into frame slots `disp_j`, then exchanged in, so `disp_j` retains the displaced old value), a **direct** row (D: a controlled permutation in place), or **mixed** (A+D) with an explicit ordered list of **elementary sub-operations** printed in §3.7.
**Slot kinds.** An **assignment slot** receives a value computed out of place and is then exchanged with its destination (it retains the displaced old value).
A **capture slot** receives a value computed out of place and is never exchanged (it retains that value as history: the arguments of `lift.call`).
The **delivery slot** of `lift.ret` is a capture slot that is subsequently exchanged, under a condition, with the destination location.

Rows with a **flag** compute it into `frame.flag` from the old state before any effect; rows with a data-dependent successor compute it into `frame. succ` before any effect; conditional-fault rows perform `faulted ^= flag`, `code ^= flag·C′` after their other effects, where C′ is the row's **effective cause** (§5.4: C′ = C, except C′ = `FAULT_UB_TRAP` when a `lift.faultif` literal C is 0).

**Frame layout** (fixed per oracle): `(old_pc : wire[P], disp_1..disp_ {k_max}, flag : wire, succ : wire[P])`, `k_max` and widths `W_j` from the widest write sets used (§4.2 lists each row's slot use).

**Dispatch.** `at_k = (pc == k)` for k = 0..n into clean scratch.

**D row**: its sub-operations in reverse order, each by its own inverse (`lift.perm_call` by the callee's adjoint; XORs, controlled flips and exchanges by themselves).

**A row**: exchange every assignment slot back with its destination **in the reverse of the forward exchange order** (the forward order is the row's listed slot order; every destination address, forward and inverse, is evaluated from the state current at that exchange, so an indexed destination such as `alloctab[atop]` is addressed with the counter value that the earlier inverse exchanges have already restored), then **uncompute every slot from the restored old state** (the same out-of-place computation, applied again as XOR, clears it).

**A+D row**: **the exact reverse of its complete §3.7 sub-operation list**, each elementary sub-operation inverted at its reversed position: a direct sub-operation by its own inverse; an assignment sub-operation by exchanging its slot back and then uncomputing the slot; a capture sub-operation by uncomputing the slot (its source has been restored by the sub-operations already undone); the delivery sub-operation by the same conditional exchanges.

**Every address and condition is evaluated from the state current at that position of the inverse** (so the `lift.ret` stack addresses and delivery condition use the callee `fp` restored one position earlier, and the `lift.call` record base uses the restored `sp`); §3.7 prints both inverse lists.
Finally uncompute `frame_t.succ` and `frame_t.flag` from the restored old state.
Uncompute every `at_k` from `pc` (which now equals the old index).
After the inverse step every frame field is clean. *(non-normative)* The forward step is a permutation Π_t; the inverse step is Π_t⁻¹ written out; T2 relies on nothing else.
B = 0 is legal: the oracle commits `FAULT_BUDGET_STEPS` on every input.
**Name resolution.** A read operand of a lifted row in an **oracle body** is a location of the oracle or a pseudo-location (an interface input or a classical argument).
A read operand in an **lproc** is a param or location of that lproc; nothing else.
Token and region parameters are usable only in their operand kinds below, not as bit-vector locations.
A written operand is a location of the containing function.
Globals and mapped interface regions are reached only by address: `w = lift.addr @g`.
Lprocs receive everything else as parameters.
An oracle declares `regs { … }`; an lproc declares five header groups:

```
  lproc @f (params..) (result) (tokens..) (classical..) (mem..)
```

The first group consists of `reg[N]` parameters, the second of exactly one `reg[T]` result location; the third consists of `token` parameters, the fourth of `iN`, `ptr` or `f64` parameters, the fifth of `region[A,W]` parameters with role `in`.
Token and classical parameters are immutable; their optional role suffixes are `token` and `classical` respectively and MUST agree with their group (§16.2).
They are not locations, stack cells or frame slots.
Classical parameters can be read as pseudo-locations (§4.7); tokens cannot be read as bits or constructed from them.
Region parameters name the passed mapped regions, not copies of their cells.
Names in all groups and `regs` are distinct.
**Argument binding.** The complete call form is `w = lift.call @f (a_1..a_m) (tokens..) (classical..) (mem..)`.
The first list supplies the location parameters using the capture and bind steps below.
The token and classical lists supply parameters from the calling oracle's `args`, or from the calling lproc's token and classical parameters, with exactly matching types.
A location (including a `reg[N]` parameter), an input wire or a literal cannot supply either list.
The region list supplies mapped interface regions of the calling oracle, or region parameters of the calling lproc, with matching `[A,W]` and `in` role.
Thus the enclosing oracle passes all three lists explicitly; a recursive or other lproc call forwards them explicitly.
The original form `w = lift.call @f (a_1..a_m)` is canonical exactly when all three additional groups are empty; otherwise all four lists are required, including empty ones.
**Fixed binding instances.** For one oracle invocation, resolve those three lists transitively to the oracle's entry arguments and mapped regions.

An instance is a pair (lproc, binding key); its key is the concatenation of the zero-based oracle `args` positions supplying its token parameters, then its classical parameters, then the zero-based oracle `mem` positions supplying its region parameters.
Compare keys lexicographically as integer sequences.

statements.text: Every prospective sum (`heap_used + max(n,1)`, `sp + R_f`, `depth + 1`) is computed at width max(operand widths) + 1 before comparison, with no wrap.
`bennett_budget` rejects limits that do not fit (§5.4).
The layout fixes no counter width: the reference realisation uses the minimum widths Hc = H + 2, Ac = A_tab + 1, Sc = S_cells + 1 and Dc = ⌈log₂(depth_limit + 2)⌉ (Dc from the invocation's budget).

Every reachable counter value fits them (heap_used ≤ heap_limit ≤ heap_limit_max < 2^H, atop ≤ 2^A_tab, fp ≤ sp ≤ stack_limit ≤ 2^S_cells, depth ≤ depth_limit ≤ 2^Dc − 2, each counter advancing only when its flag is clear), so an executor MAY use wider counters with the same F_B (§5.7); `W_cell` below uses the reference Sc.

**Initial allocator state** (oracle entry): `heap_used = 0`, bump = `heap_base`, `atop` = number of pre-entries, `sp = fp = 0`, `depth = 0`, `alloctab[0..atop)` = one pinned live entry per global in `layout. globals` order then per mapped interface region in `layout.interface_ regions` order, storage of `mem` all zero except global images.

**Locations and the result name.** Locations of a function are numbered in declaration order: an oracle's `regs`; for an lproc instance its `reg[N]` parameters, then its **result name** (`(r:reg[8])` declares a location `r` of the lproc, written like any location and read by `lift.ret`), then its `regs`.
Every location of the oracle and its instantiated closure has a global id (Did bits: index-space order of instances, then declaration order).

It is carried by an `inverse_pairs` entry (§12.3) of the certificate record of the region whose body contains the `qinplace`; an entry `{g: G, ginv: H}` covers both `qinplace @G @H` and `qinplace @H @G` (its claim checks both compositions).

An entry **covers** a `qinplace` when its `budget` is componentwise ≤ the tuple of `tk` (success at a tuple implies the same result at every larger one, §5.4), every token-typed argument's tuple equals the entry's `arg_tokens` tuple for that argument (equality: a nested oracle's outcome may change with its budget), and every other `args` value lies in its claim's `args` domain.

Its claim is an `exhaustive` claim with `expected: "inverse_pair"`, which the executor verifies as a checker does (once per closure hash, before first use), or a `structural` `inverse_pair_library` claim, which covers when the named claim of the linked library's certificate is such a claim for the same closure hashes of g and ginv (no re-execution; a library claim without an `args` domain covers every value; its proof or evidence label is the library claim's); a `sampled` claim never covers.

statements.text: `bennett_ budget` validates: `heap_limit ≤ layout.heap_limit_max`, `stack_limit ≤ 2^S_cells`, `depth_limit < 2^Dc − 1`; for a memoryless object (§7.2) `heap_limit = stack_limit = depth_limit = 0`.

B is enforced by running exactly B steps; heap, stack and depth are wire counters. *(non-normative, used by §4.5)* If the reference interpreter succeeds on x under a tuple β₀, it succeeds with the same result under every tuple β ≥ β₀ componentwise: its only limit-dependent decisions are the flags of `lift.alloc` and `lift.call`, false on that trajectory and still false with larger limits, and the step bound, not reached.
A nested `lift.oracle_call` row uses the tuple of its own token, not β, which is why §4.5 fixes those tuples exactly.

**Tokens.** A token denotes a validated tuple (B, heap_limit, stack_limit, depth_limit) and the oracle it was validated for; a region call uses the tuple of the token it is given, and a token MAY be supplied to any region call of the program (the checks above depend only on the object's layout).

Tokens come from `bennett_budget` (§10; valid until the program is unloaded) or from **`tk = budget.mint @o s h st d`** (CC and R): `@o` names an oracle of the program (a symbol reference, §9.2) whose object's layout the checks use, and is recorded with the token for diagnostics only; s, h, st, d are `i64` values read as unsigned 64-bit; the instruction applies exactly `bennett_budget`'s checks to (s, h, st, d) before any mutation; failure is a fault record `FAULT_UB_TRAP` (§4.9) and no token; success produces a fresh token for that tuple, valid until its frame is reversed or its run is CLOSED, and never constructible from an integer.
A region call given a token that is not valid is a CC trap / R fault `FAULT_UB_TRAP` before any effect (a launch argument: `E_ARG`).

A budget is classical and fixed before region entry (§3.1), so `budget.mint` is not a region instruction (§5.1).

**Effective cause.** The literal C of `fault C` (in every tier, §4.2, §4.9) and of `lift.faultif p C` records the cause C′ = C if C ≠ 0 and C′ = `FAULT_UB_TRAP` (4) if C = 0; every other row's code is a fixed nonzero constant.
So no fault is ever recorded as `FAULT_NONE`: a faulted outcome F_B(x) = (0, code) has code ≠ 0, and the fault register distinguishes it from every success (F ≥ 4 makes 4 representable).
Forward and inverse fault writes use C′.
A `lift.oracle_call` supplies a caller location `fr'`, clean when computing a fresh outcome.
No automatic propagation: the dialect emits `p = lift.icmp.ne fr' zero; lift.faultif p FAULT_CALLEE` (with `zero` a `lift.const` location) where the source requires it.

To clear `fr'`, the producer emits `lift.oracle_uncall @o` with the same token, callee, `ins` and `args` and `mem` values (no intervening row writes those locations, suite F, nor those cells, below) and the successor versions of `tgt` and `fr'`; the pair shares a dynamic invocation identity.
Alternatively `fr'` is retained until the prefix reversal.

Matching is **LIFO**: on every path, a `lift.oracle_uncall` matches the most recent preceding unmatched `lift.oracle_call` with the same callee, token, `ins`, `args` and `mem` operands (two calls followed by two uncalls form two nested pairs); an uncall that matches no call on some path, or different calls on different paths, is ill-formed.
In an lproc the match includes the fixed bindings of its instance (§3.7); parameter forwarding does not weaken any matching or cleanup condition.

Suite F rejects a pair when a row on a path between them writes one of its `ins` locations; an intervening `lift.store` is not ill-formed (its address is data): `lift.oracle_uncall` is the same permutation as the call (§4.2), so a pair whose cells changed in between still executes and is undone by the prefix reversal, and clearing `fr'` is then the producer's obligation.
**Requirement.** A region's completed operation equals its declared operation ⊗ identity on every borrowed bundle and on any external system entangled with it.

**Rule (suite F).** Borrowed wires (set B) are touched (as control or target) only inside **borrow frames**: maximal contiguous permutation- only subcircuits from the first to the last instruction touching B.

The frame's realised permutation P_F on its wires MUST factor as `P_F = P' ⊗ I_B`, established by a T3 claim over the frame's full domain (exhaustive, or a library certificate, §12 `borrow_frames`) or **structurally by the translation lemma**: the frame is `V; W; V⁻¹; W` where
(i) every gate of V is an X-family flip (`x cx ccx mcx`) whose **target is in B** and whose **controls are all in a set X with X ∩ B = ∅**; V touches no other wire; hence V maps b ↦ b ⊕ v(X);
(ii) every gate of W is an X-family flip whose **target is outside X, outside B, and outside the set of all controls of W** (as sets, over the whole of W), and W writes no wire of X;
(iii) every gate of W has **at most one control in B**;
(iv) V⁻¹ is the exact reverse sequence of V; no `swap` appears in the frame.
Then W's effect is affine in b, the net map is t ⊕= Σ_g c_g(Y)·v_{j(g)}(X), independent of b, and b is restored (the dirty-ancilla MCX pattern).

Suite F contains the negative tests `cx b y; cx y z; cx b y` (V;W;V⁻¹), `V = cx b2 b1, W = cx b1 t` (b2 ∈ B, violates X ∩ B = ∅), `V = cx b x` (target outside B), and `W = swap y z; cx b y` (swap excluded).
Oracles are one frame verified by their own T3 claim over D.
Inlining, structure recovery, dispatch re-indexing and simplification MUST produce on every x ∈ D the same final interface tuple as §5.2's construction on the reference body (T6).

statements.text: Every workspace bundle version, location version and cell version has provenance `perm` (computed by permutation gates from its **dependency set** S of versions) or `other`.
Cell versions `(region, i, v)` advance on every write.
Π is the effective control context at the instruction.
`qalloc` | perm, S = ∅
`d = qcopy s` | d: perm, S = {s} ∪ Π
`d = qload r a` | d: perm, S = {a} ∪ cells(r) ∪ Π
`qxor s t` | t: perm with S_t ∪ S_s ∪ Π if both perm, else other
`qexch a b` | each output: perm with S_a ∪ S_b ∪ Π if both perm, else other
`qstore r a v` | each cell (r,i): version advances; perm with S_cell ∪ S_v ∪ {a} ∪ Π if both perm, else other
`qexchm r a v` | v and every cell: perm with S_v ∪ ⋃S_cells ∪ {a} ∪ Π if all perm, else other; cell versions advance
permutation gate, controls C, target t | t: perm with S_t ∪ C ∪ ⋃S_c ∪ Π iff t was perm, else other
diagonal gate on u | unchanged
non-diagonal gate on u | u: other; closes the window of every value whose S contains u
`oracle_call @o (ins) tgt fr (mem)` | tgt, fr: perm with S = ins ∪ {tgt, fr} ∪ cells(every region passed) ∪ Π; `in` regions unchanged
`lift.perm_call` / permutation `action_call` | each mut: perm with S = mut ∪ ins ∪ cells(regions passed) ∪ Π; `mut`-region cells advance with the same S
non-permutation `action_call` | every mut and every `mut`-region cell: other
`qinplace @g @ginv tk x (ins) (mem) (args)` | x: perm with S_x ∪ ins ∪ cells(every region in `mem`) ∪ Π if x was perm, else other; the `ins` wires and `mem` cells are unchanged
lifted rows | each written location/cell: perm with the union of its read operands' sets ∪ Π; written cells' versions advance

A perm value g with set S is **in its window** from its computation until the first of: a non-diagonal gate on a wire in S or in g; a version advance of a cell in S; a non-permutation action call touching a wire in S; a permutation change to a wire in S not undone before g's cleanup.
Each cleanup is bound to its exact computing sequence and requires the versions that sequence read to be current.
Every perm value MUST be cleaned within its window and before its region exits; otherwise the region is **ill-formed** (closed-window measurement-based cleanup is not admitted).
`other` values are released only by the adjoint of the sequence that produced them.

Cleaning g within its window returns g's wires to |0⟩ and factorises them from the remaining state; diagonal uses of g or of its dependencies have applied the corresponding diagonal phases to the remainder, which is part of the program's declared semantics.

Every cleanup in this version is **unitary**: realisation `reverse` (the adjoint of g's exact computing sequence, §6.2) or `recompute` (legal for `perm` values only: recompute g into a fresh clean bundle by the same sequence, `qxor` it into g's wires, uncompute the fresh bundle by the adjoint).

**Measurement-based cleanup is not admitted in sched/ cert 0.9**: a schedule naming any other realisation is invalid, the target capability `mbu` is reserved and MUST be `false`, and no cleanup produces a `channel` claim. *(non-normative)* The fixup after an X-basis measurement of g with outcome m is the phase (−1)^{m·g(x)}, a function of g's computing sequence and not of the target; its normative form, its controlled variant and its certificate kind are deferred (§17 item 6; default: unitary cleanup).

Schedules and certificate cleanup entries are keyed by `(region hash, variant, inherited control count)`; a region reachable under a non-empty control context MUST have a cleanup schedule for that key.

T4 is stated over the logical history.
**Active and audit history.** The *active* history is the sequence of frames not marked reversed; reversed frames and `uncall` markers remain as immutable *audit records*.
Undoing a defining frame removes its dynamic instance from the active environment although its audit record is retained.

**Pure frames.** A frame is **pure** iff it belongs to `br` or to a defining instruction among `const`, the binops, `udiv..srem`, `icmp`, `select`, `zext sext trunc`, `ptrtoint inttoptr`, `load`, `qreg.width qreg.id qreg.from_id`: it changes only the set of instances.
Every other frame (`store alloc free call ret uncall trap fault effect hostcall qreg.new qreg.free qreg.slice qreg.concat measure budget.mint`, region calls, fault records) is impure.

**History traversal** (the one reversal procedure, used by segment `uncall` and by whole-run reversal). A range of frames is **reversed** by visiting its frames in LIFO order; a frame already marked reversed and an `uncall` frame are **skipped**; every other frame is undone by its row of the table above and then marked reversed.
Reversed frames stay in the history, marked, and are never undone again.

An `uncall` marker is always skipped: when a later traversal (an enclosing segment's `uncall`, or whole-run reversal) reaches it, the frames of the segment it names are already marked and are skipped too, so neither the marker nor its segment is undone, re-executed or redone a second time.
**Segment uncall** (`uncall @f (args) (results)`).
Let S be the most recent completed call segment of the history (a `call` frame, its matching `ret` frame and every frame between them).

The `uncall` is legal iff S is a call of `@f`, S's recorded boundary argument and result values equal the operand values, **every frame after S is pure**, and S contains, at any nesting depth, **no `measure` frame** and no `qreg. free` frame whose cleanliness was not verified (hardware, §17 item 14); otherwise it is a CC trap / R fault `FAULT_UB_TRAP` and changes nothing beyond the fault record (§4.9).

Execution reverses S by the history traversal (nested segments are undone; nested segments already cancelled by an inner `uncall`, and that inner `uncall` frame, are skipped), and pushes an `uncall` frame naming S.
The instances defined inside S no longer exist; using such a name before it is redefined is a CC trap / R fault `FAULT_UB_TRAP`.

**Whole-run reversal** (§10) is the history traversal over the whole history: S's effects on memory, the allocation table, devices, the register ledger and tokens were undone by the `uncall`, and the frames between S and the `uncall` are pure, so at the `uncall` frame every component except the retained instances already equals its value before S.
T4 is stated over these frames. *(non-normative)* S is never re-executed and never redone; the compute–copy–`uncall` idiom derives what it keeps through pure instructions before the `uncall`.
Suite A contains: `f` calls `g`, uncalls `g`, returns; `g` performs one `clock.read`; `call f; uncall f` leaves the clock at its entry value; and `uncall` of a segment that measured is a trap.
A target is a JSON document in RFC 8785 canonical form; `target_hash` = SHA-256 of those bytes; numbers are exact rationals from their decimal text.
Cost expressions are a closed JSON AST:

```
  expr := number | {"var": v} | {"op": o, "args": [expr, …]} | {"table": name, "index": "k" | "eps_decade"}
  v    := "k" | "c" | "eps" | "a" | "w" | "i" | "theta"
  o    := "+" (2) | "-" (2) | "*" (2) | "/" (2) | "max" (2) | "min" (2) | "ceil" (1) | "log2inv_eps" (0)
```
`log2inv_eps` = the exact integer min{ j ≥ 0 : eps · 2^j ≥ 1 } for 0 < eps ≤ 1; eps outside (0, 1] is a load-time error; an entry with `epsilon` 0 MUST NOT reference `eps` or `log2inv_eps`.
Division by zero and a table index outside the array are load-time errors.
Costs MUST be nonnegative and finite.
**EPS-DECADE** (K9; source: bennett-vm-cxg). A table expression with `index: "eps_decade"` evaluates its zero-based array index as the exact integer min{ j ≥ 0 : eps · 10^j ≥ 1 }.
It requires a context binding `eps` and 0 < eps ≤ 1; otherwise it is a load-time error.
Thus it uses the requested `epsilon_share`, not the entry's achieved `epsilon`.
Evaluation uses exact rational comparisons, never a floating-point logarithm.
The existing out-of-array rule applies to this integer.
An entry with `epsilon` 0 MUST NOT use `eps_decade`, including through a table lookup.
This extends the exact-entry prohibition above; it does not assign an index to eps = 0.

statements.text: Imports must match all five groups; validation and instance formation are repeated after linking (§9.3).
**Canonical function bytes**: the text from the function's header line through its last instruction line, lines joined by LF, no trailing LF.
**Semantic envelope** of a symbol (byte-exact; every part ends with LF):

```
  (1) "isa=" <full version string, e.g. 0.9>
  (2) "ptr_width=" INT
  (3) the JCS signature
  (4) the canonical function bytes (with reference tokens replaced, below); for a data symbol: its data line NAME SP HEX
  (5a) for every data entry in the closure set, sorted by name bytewise:        "data " NAME " " HEX
  (5b) for every layout leaf in the closure set, sorted by dotted path bytewise: "layout " <dotted path> " " <JCS value>
  (5c) for an R/CC function, for every device model and service it uses, sorted: "device " <name> " " <JCS entry>
  (6) for every referenced symbol outside the symbol's SCC, in order of first reference: its 64-hex hash
```
**Closure set**, by symbol kind.

**Oracle**: **all** `layout` leaves of the object except `interface_regions` entries of other oracles (every global's pre-entry affects its allocation faults), its own `interface_ regions.<oracle>.*` leaves, and every data image those leaves name.
**Lproc**: the leaves and images of every global `@g` it names in `lift. addr`.
**Action / permutation action**: no layout leaves; the `@image` of each `qregion` is an ordinary symbol reference (replaced in part (4), listed in part (6)).
**CC / R function**: all `layout` leaves, every data image they name, and in (5c) every device model and `hostcall` service it uses.
**Data symbol**: parts (5)–(6) are empty.

A layout leaf is a scalar or an object at the deepest level the schema lists (`globals. <name>` and `interface_regions.<oracle>.<region>` are leaves; `ptr_ width`, `H`, … are leaves); a scalar's JCS value is its decimal text.

**Globals are data symbols**: every global `g` in `layout.globals` MUST have `image` = `g` and the object MUST define a `data` symbol named `g` of that size, so the token `@g` in `lift.addr` is both the global and a symbol reference (replaced by the data symbol's hash; the global's `base` and `size` enter through the layout leaf).
An `@name` naming an interface region (in `lift.addr`) is not a symbol reference and is left unchanged.

**Reference replacement**: in parts (4)–(5) every `@name` symbol-reference token is replaced by `@` followed by the referenced symbol's 64-hex hash (the symbol's own name in its header line is a definition, not a reference, and is left unchanged); the **interface hash** uses interface hashes of defined symbols and `SHA-256(name ‖ 0x00 ‖ JCS signature)` (hex) for unresolved imports; the **closure hash** uses closure hashes.
**Acyclic and cyclic symbols.** The reference graph has an edge from a symbol to every symbol it references (parts (4)–(5)).

An **acyclic** symbol — a one-member SCC that does not reference itself — has hash = SHA-256 of its own envelope (example 1's `inc8`, example 2's `zero` and `sum_db`); the SCC procedure below applies to every **cyclic** SCC, including a one-member SCC whose function references itself (example 2's `sum`).

**SCCs**: members ordered by name bytewise; every intra- SCC `@name` token (parts (4)–(5)) is replaced by `@$<decimal index>`; intra-SCC references contribute no part-(6) line; `scc_hash` = SHA-256 over the concatenation of the members' envelopes in that order; member hash = SHA-256 over the ASCII bytes of `<scc_hash hex>:<decimal index>`. **object_hash** = SHA-256 of the canonical object text with the `schedule`, `certificate` and `coverage` sections deleted together with the blank line preceding each.
`reference_program_hash` = the oracle's interface hash.

statements.text: **Model.** A run executes a device CC entry; the host passes classical arguments, register ids and the entropy tape, receives classical results, fault codes and declared measurements; host services are reached by `hostcall`.

**Positional binding**: argument i of `bennett_ run` binds to parameter i of the entry's signature: `INT(width, bytes)` to `iN` with width = N (else `E_ARG`), `F64` to `f64`, `QREG` to `qreg[n]` with the register's n or to `qreg[*]` with any width, `TOKEN` to `token` (a valid token, §5.4).
Arguments and the entropy tape are **copied** at `bennett_run`; the caller may free its buffers afterwards.
Host-minted tokens are scoped to the program and destroyed at unload; device-minted tokens to their run (§5.4).
Accessor-returned pointers are valid until the owning object is freed.
`bennett_unload` with a run not CLOSED: `E_INVALID_STATE`.

**Invocation tree.** A run record is a tree (CC segments, R calls, Q calls); an R call's subtree is owned by its R history; `bennett_reverse` reverses post-order: CC segments by their run history, R calls by LIFO reversal of their history (§7.4, reversed segments and `uncall` frames skipped), top-level Q calls by re-application / adjoint.
A fault record is terminal (§4.9): the run is `FAILED`, and every activation open at the fault keeps its frames, which reversal undoes like those of a call that returned.

**States.** `CREATED → RUNNING → (SUSPENDED ⇄ RUNNING) → (HOST_REQUEST ⇄ RUNNING) → COMPLETED | FAILED`; `COMPLETED → REVERSED`; `FAILED → REVERSED`; any of `COMPLETED/FAILED/REVERSED → CLOSED` (`bennett_run_close` releases the record; register ids created by the run remain valid unless measured or freed).

A run owns the registers and memory it touches exclusively while not CLOSED; a register reached by `qreg.from_id` is touched from then on; `bennett_qreg_prepare`, `bennett_qreg_free` and a `bennett_run` argument naming a register owned by another run that is not CLOSED are `E_INVALID_STATE`.

**Reverse eligibility**: `COMPLETED` or `FAILED`; no `measure` frame; no `qreg.free` frame whose cleanliness was not verified (§17 item 14); no register it touched has been prepared, freed, sliced or used by another run since; else `E_NOT_REVERSIBLE`.

Reversing a `FAILED` run first undoes its terminal fault record, then traverses the rest of its history exactly as for a completed run, including the frames of activations that never returned; the run is then `REVERSED` with every component T4 names at its entry value.

`bennett_qreg_prepare` and `bennett_ qreg_free` require a clean register (`E_QREG_NOT_CLEAN` otherwise on a verifying executor; a non-verifying one: §17 item 14); there is no reset and no trace-out: a register in unknown state is released by a `measure` inside a run, which consumes its handle (§3.3).

**Results.** `bennett_result_get` writes value i and sets `*kind` and `*width`: `INT` as ⌈N/8⌉ little-endian bytes, `*width` = N; `F64` as the 8 IEEE 754 binary64 little-endian bytes, `*width` = 64; `QREG` and `TOKEN` as the 8-byte little-endian id, `*width` = 64.
A `cap` smaller than that byte count is `E_ARG` and nothing is written.
Fault records are read by `bennett_result_nfaults` / `bennett_result_fault` (codes of §4.9; a `COMPLETED` run has none, a `FAILED` run has exactly one, its terminal record, and exposes no values).

For an R `fault C`, `bennett_wait` returns `OK` with `*result_out` set and `*request_out` NULL as for any `FAILED` run; `bennett_result_nvalues` is 0, `bennett_result_nfaults` is 1 and `bennett_result_fault(result, 0)` is exactly C when C ≠ 0 (4 when C = 0, §5.4), with all 64 bits preserved.
The fault code is result data, not a `bennett_status` error or a host-service reply.

**Waiting.** `bennett_wait` blocks until the run leaves `RUNNING` and returns `OK` with exactly one outcome: `HOST_REQUEST` (`*request_out` set, `*result_out` NULL; `bennett_reply` answers it and the run is `RUNNING` again) or `COMPLETED` / `FAILED` (`*result_out` set, `*request_ out` NULL).
Waiting on a `SUSPENDED`, `REVERSED` or `CLOSED` run is `E_ INVALID_STATE`.

**`hostcall`.** `rlen = hostcall service ptr len`: `[ptr, ptr + len)` MUST lie in one live allocation (else CC trap and no request is made); those bytes are copied into the request; the run enters `HOST_REQUEST`; the reply payload is written to `[ptr, ptr + min(len, reply length))` and `rlen` = the full reply length (so truncation is detectable; a reply whose length does not fit `ptr_width` bits is refused by `bennett_reply` with `E_ARG` before any write, and the run stays in `HOST_REQUEST`); the frame records the request bytes, the overwritten bytes and the reply bytes.
Every `service` is declared in `devices.services`; an undeclared one is a load error.

**Tape.** `bennett_tape_next` yields each `effect` in tape order; `args` holds the operation's operands in the order of §7.3, each an unsigned 64-bit little-endian field (pointers zero-extended from `ptr_width`), so `*alen` = 8 × arity.

**Generated operations and the expansion library.** Every row and instruction expands into **generated operations** (gates, allocations, releases).
Above gate level the order is fixed by §3.6, §4.2, §4.5–§4.6 and §5.2 (dispatch comparators k = 0..n in index order; a row's sub-operations in listed order; successor XORs; commit; cleanup).

Below that level (the gate decomposition of comparators, adders, multiplexers, `inrange` scans and their scratch) the expansion is defined by an **expansion library**: a versioned document, identified in the schedule's `bindings.expansion` as `{ "name", "version", "hash" }`, that lists for every row kind and every instruction its generated operations in order, with their **ordinals**, scratch identities and the subset it marks removable, and that is extensionally equal to the reference (§5.7, T6).
A consumer that does not implement the bound library rejects the schedule (`E_SCHEDULE_INFEASIBLE`); two consumers implementing it execute and charge the same operation set.

**Matching.** Every generated operation has an **invocation chain**: the program points of the region calls, `lift.call`s and `lift.oracle_call`s that led to it, outermost first, ending in its own point.

`path` matches an operation iff it is a **prefix** of that chain, element by element: `symbol` and `point` equal, and `iteration` either `*` or equal to the vector of 0-based dynamic repetition counts of the `qloop`s enclosing that point (outermost first; its length is the point's loop nesting depth, `[]` outside every loop).

`step` is the forward machine step t ∈ 1..B of an oracle-generated operation (`phase: rev` denotes the inverse of step t; both are per invocation level, so a nested oracle's step is selected by a path element for the nested call); `generated` is the ordinal within the row's expansion in the bound library.

**Specificity** is the lexicographic tuple (path length, number of non-`*` iterations, step non-`*`, phase non-`*`, generated non-`*`); an entry applies to a generated operation iff all its selectors match; among matching entries the unique maximal one applies; **two incomparable maximal matching entries make the schedule invalid** (document order is never significant).
Selectors are resolved independently per `kind`.

Defaults for uncovered operations: `reverse`; `native` if the gate matches a `gates` entry, else the first matching scheme; class = the first class declared in the target's `classes` object (JCS order) that has capacity for it; sequential timing in generated order.
**Timing**: a `start` time MUST be ≥ the end of every operation the operation depends on (data, wire lifetime, region cell version, effect order); an entry violating this makes the schedule invalid.

statements.text: The JSON file is RFC 8785 canonical UTF-8, with no trailing LF, containing exactly `isa`, `name`, `version` and `recipes`.
The first three are strings `0.9`, `ref`, `0.9`.
`recipes` is an array in bytewise `kind` order, then increasing parameter tuple order.
Each instantiated recipe has `kind`, its integer width or other named integer parameters, `operations`, `scratch`, `removable` and `source` (the motivating ISA sentence).
A parameterised recipe uses `parameters` (an ordered array of formals defined below) and `body` instead of the instance's `operations`; its body uses the closed constructors below.
Recipes cover every §4 instruction/row, the §3.6 step, §3.7 activation operations and §5.2 construction, with no implementation-private leaf.
Classical instructions/effects remain classical leaf events (§8.2), not invented quantum gates.
The README documents schema, parameters, coverage and witnesses; it is not hashed and cannot alter operations.

The library hash is SHA-256 of this UTF-8 envelope (every line ends LF, including the last); the fourth line is the **entire** canonical library JSON, including all recipes, sources and versions, without an embedded hash field:

```
isa=0.9
expansion=ref
version=0.9
<JCS library document>
```
`bindings.expansion` names `ref`, version `0.9`, and this 64-lowercase-hex hash.

This adopts §9.2's version-prefixed, LF-terminated **envelope convention**, with explicit expansion-domain and library-version lines; it is a new library rule, not §9.2's symbol signature/SCC envelope.
Motivation (0.8 §11): "a versioned document, identified in the schedule's `bindings.expansion` as { name, version, hash }"; 0.8 §9.2: "Semantic envelope ... every part ends with LF".
A changed recipe, source, scratch name or ordering changes the library hash; no schedule/certificate can silently inherit that change (§12.1's realised-subject binding).

**Expansion and ordinals.** Recipe bodies are ordered arrays of constructors: a gate (`gate`, ordered `wires`, optional `params`), an allocation (`alloc`, `width`, `class`, `state`), release (`release`), classical event (`classical`, `point`), counted loop (`for`, `from`, `to`, `body`), named recipe expansion (`invoke`, ordered `args`), or inverse (`inverse`, `body`).
Constructor objects have exactly those keys.
Fully instantiated `operations` contain only emitted leaves, each also carrying its computed `ordinal`; unexpanded `body` constructors carry no ordinal.
Scalars are integer literals, parameter names, or prefix arrays `[op, operands…]` for `+ - * div mod bit`; div is floor division with a positive divisor.
`bit(x,i)` requires nonnegative integers x and i and returns floor(x/2^i) mod 2, with no fixed machine-word truncation (K23).
For x=13, bit(x,0..4) is 1,0,1,1,0; literal construction emits X only for the one bits, in increasing bit order.
Wires are declaration names with integer-expression subscripts.
Loops enumerate [from,to) in increasing order; expansion is depth first, array order, and recipe dependencies are acyclic.
An inverse reverses its fully expanded body and adjoints each leaf by §5.3, interchanging allocation/release.
The complete serialized catalog must encode the algorithms below in these constructors before release; this draft does not claim that prose alone is an interchangeable file.

**Typed binding (K19).** A formal is `{ "name": name, "type": type }`, with exactly these keys, except `wire`, which additionally requires `width`, and `templates`, which additionally requires `length` (integer expressions using earlier integer formals); `arguments` requires `symbol`, and `value` requires `isa_type`, as specified in K24; K25–K27 add `records`, `region`, `class`, and `allocation` with the keys specified there.
Types are `integer`, `wire`, `angle`, `body`, `symbol`, `environment`, `event`, `image`, `templates`, `arguments`, `value`, `records`, `region`, `class`, and `allocation`.
A bare name abbreviates an `integer` formal, retaining the printed witness bytes.
Names are unique within a parameter list.
Width expressions use only earlier integer formals.
A wire formal of width n is the ordered list w[n], with little-endian indexing, including the empty list when n = 0.
`invoke` binds `args` positionally, evaluating actuals in the caller's lexical environment before binding any callee formal.

statements.text: Integer actuals use the scalar grammar above.

A wire actual is a wire name, a subscripted wire, an array of wire actuals concatenated left to right, or exactly `{ "range": name, "from": scalar, "to": scalar }`, selecting [from,to) from a named bundle; bounds must satisfy 0 ≤ from ≤ to ≤ its width.
An actual's resulting length must equal its formal's evaluated width.
In a gate's `wires` array a whole formal emits all its wires in order; this encodes `mcx(k)` as k controls followed by one target, including k=0.
`{ "each": name, "in": actual, "body": [...] }` additionally visits wire-list elements in order, binding name as a one-wire formal for each visit.
Its binding shadows lexically and is restored after the loop.
A body actual is an ordered constructor array, captured with its caller's lexical environment, or the name of an existing body formal.
Exactly `{ "splice": name }` expands it at that point.

An inverse traverses constructors in reverse, toggles the adjoint on nested bodies and uses the same restored bindings at each position; allocation declarations supply release/adjoint metadata even when allocation and release occur in different nested constructor lists.
A symbol actual is a 64-lowercase-hex §9.2 closure hash, or a bound symbol formal.
The linked closure registry supplies that symbol's own typed interface and constructor body; the hash must match the linked closure, not an arbitrary supplied body.
Exactly `{ "call": name, "args": [...] }` expands that symbol under a new invocation-path element identified by the call constructor's expansion occurrence.

statements.text: It retains its own ordinal space starting at zero.
`invoke` is recipe composition within a row; `call` is a semantic symbol invocation and never flattens callee ordinals into the caller's space.
Repeated calls have distinct paths.
The inherited effective-control set is always passed to callees and body splices.
An `environment` actual uses the wire-actual grammar and adds its wires to that set (set union, repeated controls counted once).
Exactly `{ "under": actual, "body": [...] }` adds controls for its lexical body and restores the outer set afterwards.
Controls apply to semantic gates only, never allocation/release or classical events (§3.5/§4.3).
A control may coincide with a gate's explicit control, but never with a target (including a diagonal-gate target), as §3.3 requires.
Gate operands must otherwise be distinct.
An `event` actual is exactly `{ "instruction": text, "point": text }`, or an event formal name.
`instruction` is one complete canonical §9.1 classical instruction with its operand bindings; `point` identifies its §8.2 classical execution point.

`{ "classical": opcode, "point": event_name }` emits that bound event (its opcode must match, allowing a concrete `.iN` width suffix) without executing or substituting its instruction text; classical semantics and retained history are §4.1/§7.4.
Literal classical leaves retain their existing `classical`/`point` form.
A classical event is not a unitary; an `inverse` containing one requires retained §7.4 history and is not a quantum-library matrix witness.

Consumers MUST reject the library document on arity/type/width mismatch, unbound name or closure hash, invalid wire range, duplicate formal, nonfinite angle, unknown constructor/key/gate, invalid gate arity, coincident target/control, unmatched allocation/release, or cyclic `invoke`/symbol expansion.
Static integer bounds must yield finite expansion; validation is repeated for every actual parameter tuple before its expansion can be used.
There are no implicit bindings or defaults.
Acyclicity concerns declared recipe/symbol dependencies, not repetition of a higher-order recipe name inside finite captured actual syntax: qloop(3, qloop(2, B)) expands to six copies of B.
Consumers expand finite actual bodies to a constructor fixpoint.

statements.text: **Image binding (K21).** An `image` actual is a bound image formal or an even-length string of lowercase hexadecimal byte pairs in data-image byte order.
The empty string denotes the absent/default-zero image, including on a wire list whose width is not byte-aligned.

Exactly `{ "image": name, "wires": actual }` emits no leaf for the empty image; a nonempty image requires exactly eight wires per byte; bit 8j+i of the flattened wire list is bit i of byte j (i=0..7).
It emits one X leaf for each one bit in increasing bit order, with an empty effective-control set regardless of inherited controls.
This constructor denotes only the unconditional data-image preparation or restoration required by §3.5/§4.6; ordinary X gates remain semantic.
The bytes are serialized in the actual, not resolved from an unbound external image name.
Image leaves have ordinary row ordinals and the same allocation wire identities as semantic leaves.
Inverse traverses these X leaves in reverse order, still unconditional.
Reject malformed hex, unbound image or a byte/wire width mismatch.
Witness: `"8102"` on 16 wires emits X at indices 0,7,9; inverse emits 9,7,0, even under a false inherited predicate.
This fixes the image binding bytes without altering §9.2's source data-symbol identity.
**Indexed typed body templates (K22).** A `templates` actual is an ordered array of exactly `length` objects, each with exactly `parameters` and `body`, or the name of a bound templates formal.
Each object's parameters use the same typed formal grammar as recipes; its body uses the same closed constructors.
The array is captured in the caller's lexical environment.

Exactly `{ "apply": name, "index": scalar, "args": [...] }` selects its zero-based element and binds positional actuals evaluated at the apply site, with the same type/width/arity validation as invoke.
Formal bindings shadow captured names only inside that application; all free references still resolve in the captured environment.
Effective controls are the union of captured controls, apply-site controls and explicit environment actuals.
Fresh allocations include the application occurrence in their identity.

statements.text: Applications compose within the containing row's ordinal space; they do not introduce a semantic symbol call.
Reject negative/out-of-range indices, length mismatch, unknown/duplicate formals or invalid constructor syntax even in unused templates.
Inverse reverses the applications and adjoints each selected body using its restored positional bindings.
This permits row templates with a typed frame formal, applied to frame_t, and a step template applied to each successive frame without rebinding a captured free name.
Witness: two templates `(f:wire[2])` containing CX outer f[0] and CX outer f[1], applied in index order to a, emit CX outer a[0], CX outer a[1]; the inverse emits them in reverse order.
Applying to a one-wire actual rejects.
Applying the same template to distinct frame slices cannot change its captured outer binding.
**Closure-bound argument vectors (K24).** An `arguments` formal's `symbol` names an earlier symbol formal.
Its actual is an array of actuals in that linked symbol's own formal order, or a bound arguments name for the identical closure hash.
The vector captures the actuals' lexical environment; validate every argument against that symbol's interface at binding, even when no call executes.
`call` additionally accepts the bound arguments name as its `args` value; it forwards the whole vector without reinterpreting names in the forwarding recipe's scope.
Reject a vector bound to another closure, even if the two interfaces have equal widths.
Each call still has its own invocation path and callee ordinals.
A `value` formal's `isa_type` is `iN` (N a canonical positive decimal), `f64`, `token`, or exactly `{ "ptr": N }` with N the linked object's positive `ptr_width`.

Values use exactly §12.3 invocation encodings: canonical unsigned decimal strings within the iN/ptr range, binary64 bit-pattern hex (including signed zero and NaN payloads for classical f64), or four canonical nonnegative decimal strings for a token tuple.
A value may also be the name of a bound value of exactly the same `isa_type`; widening or converting it implicitly is forbidden.
Token values carry tuples, never process-local ids.
This adds no arithmetic on classical f64 or tokens inside a recipe.
A forwarding recipe `(S:symbol,A:arguments(S))` with two calls using A preserves all bindings and emits two distinct invocation paths starting at ordinal zero.
Swapping a and b rejects; 2^128 for i128, a three-part token, or an arguments vector for a different closure rejects.
This binding rule does not replace §3.3's source interface region shape/role validation or the §9.2 linker obligation that the registry interface and body match the supplied closure hash.
**Ordered descriptors (K25).** A `records` formal has exactly `name`, `type`, `fields`, `order`.
`fields` is an ordered typed formal list; its types are `integer`, `wire`, `region`, `class`, `allocation`, or `image` (K21, for source data-image descriptors).
A field's width/shape expressions may use enclosing earlier integer formals and earlier integer fields, never later fields.
`order` is an array of distinct integer field names.
An actual is an array of objects whose keys are exactly the field names, or a bound records name with the identical field schema and order.
Each field actual resolves in the actual's captured lexical environment; earlier integer fields additionally bind width/shape expressions.
Forwarding preserves resolved identities, revalidates widths against the receiving enclosing integers, and never resolves a wire name again.
With nonempty `order`, the tuples of those fields must be strictly increasing lexicographically; with empty `order`, array order is normative.
Empty arrays are valid.
`{"visit": name, "body": [...]}` visits records in array order, binding all their fields lexically for that body, shadowing outer names across all types and restoring them afterwards.
An inverse visits the same records in reverse order and adjoints each body.
No record iteration emits a leaf by itself.
Reject extra/missing fields, an invalid schema, order mismatch, duplicate/out-of-order keys, or any invalid field actual, even for an unvisited list.
Record iteration and K22 template application share the same capture, effective-control and occurrence-identity rules.
The following descriptor schemas bind source metadata, rather than caller-supplied circuit bodies.

Byte `base+j` is exactly wires `cells[8*j .. 8*j+8)`.

An activation location list has `id`, `width`, `slot` integers followed by `location:wire[width]`, ordered by `id`.
The ids and widths are exactly §3.7's global ids and declared widths.

For a selected instance, `slot` is its zero-based declaration index in L_f, including parameters and the result name; for a closure delivery list it is the declaration index within the location's own instance.
A capture list has `position`, `width` integers followed by `source:wire[width]`, `parameter:wire[width]`, `capture:wire[width]`, ordered by `position`.
Positions are 0..m-1 in source argument order; parameter and capture are the corresponding callee location and frame displacement slot.
The stack low-width slice for location slot j starts at `(old_sp+3+j)*W_cell` in C2 and `(restored_fp+3+j)*W_cell` in R3; higher cell bits are untouched.
Delivery scans the complete closure list in global id order.
Reject records inconsistent with those source mappings.
These lists add no locations for token/classical/region arguments; those remain K24/K26 fixed bindings.
A construction state list has `width`, `initial` integers, `I:image`, `storage:allocation`, with empty `order` (array order).
Each storage identity is distinct, clean and exactly `width` bits; its class is `any` for the implicit §5.2 state.

In allocation order the list is: pc, pc-prime, faulted, code, result_val; then heap_used, atop, sp, fp, depth, ordinary mem, stack when layout state exists; locations in global id order; local regions in declaration order; alloctab when layout state exists; frames 0..B-1.
Omit only the layout state excluded by §7.2's memoryless-object rule.
Counter widths/values are the reference widths and initial values of §3.7; all other non-image initial values are zero except alloctab pre-entries.
A table cell packs base[ptr_width], size[ptr_width], live, pinned, in that LSB-first order; pre-entries are in §3.7's layout order and unused entries are zero.
Image-bearing mem and local regions have initial=0.
Ordinary mem's I is exactly 2^H bytes, initially zero, with each global's image overlaid at its layout base; bytes hidden by mapped interface regions remain zero.
A local region's I is its exact bound data image, or empty for absent/default zero.
Every other record has I empty and initial the nonnegative integer encoding of its initial bit vector, strictly below 2^width.
Mapped interface regions are borrowed inputs, never acquired by this state list.

A separate frame list has `index` integer and `frame:allocation`, ordered by index; it contains exactly B entries indexed 0..B-1, referring to the identical frame handles in the state list, each with §3.6's fixed frame width and field order.
Reject any mismatch of source state, image, width, class, order or identity.

The construction acquires/initializes this list, invokes the catalog `step` once per frame, commits, then reverses frames and initialization before releasing the list in reverse order; source row/successor templates supply rows, never a replacement dispatcher or construction body.

Visiting X on each first bit emits X a[0], X b[0]; inverse emits X b[0], X a[0].

Exchanging the two record positions rejects for id order.

statements.text: To make Boolean recipes deterministic, use no common-subexpression elimination: visit every Boolean expression tree in left-to-right postorder, giving each internal node a fresh clean scratch bit.
NOT(a) uses X d; CX a d, XOR(a,b) uses CX a d; CX b d, AND(a,b) uses CCX a b d.
OR(a,b) is the ordered tree XOR(XOR(a,b),AND(a,b)); repeated operands are separate tree occurrences (coincident AND operands reduce to a single CX so the gate has distinct operands).
XOR the root into the destination, then reverse all compute gates and release scratch in reverse allocation order.
Constants are zero or X of a clean bit.
All formulas use old source values captured before an assignment/exchange.

External effective controls apply to the resulting semantic gates, not allocations; scratch computations may be unconditional provided their compute/uncompute pair is balanced when the external control is false (§3.5, §4.3).
Copy, XOR, exchange; native gates | `qxor`: CX s[i] t[i]; `qcopy`: allocate then the same; `quncopy`: the same then release; `qexch`: SWAP a[i] b[i].
Keep each §4.4 gate as a leaf; target schemes expand later. | §4.5: "`cx s[i] t[i]`" and "`swap a[i] b[i]`"; §8.3: "Every template gate MUST itself match a gates entry".
Ripple add/sub and comparisons | c[0]=0; p[i]=a[i] XOR b[i]; sum[i]=p[i] XOR c[i]; c[i+1]=(a[i] AND b[i]) XOR (p[i] AND c[i]); compute each bit in this order, XOR sums out, reverse scratch.
Subtraction adds bitwise NOT b with c[0]=1.
Unsigned a<b is NOT the final subtraction carry; equality is the AND of NOT(a[i] XOR b[i]) in increasing-bit left-associated order.

`ule` is OR(ult,eq); signed comparison selects sign(a) if signs differ, else ult. | §17 item 7: "ripple-carry adders and comparators"; §4.1: "wrap"; §3.7: prospective sums use "no wrap" (retain the extra carry for those).
Other arithmetic, casts, select | AND/XOR/OR use the Boolean trees above; select emits ((NOT p) AND b[i]) XOR (p AND a[i]).
Multiply folds shifted partial products in increasing multiplier-bit order through ripple add modulo 2^N.
Shifts scan shift amounts j=0..N−1, equality-selecting the corresponding source bit; ≥N produces zero.
Sign-extend replicates the high source bit, zero-extend supplies zero, truncate drops high bits.

Division uses restoring unsigned long division, scanning dividend bits from N−1 to 0: append that bit to an N+1-bit remainder, compare with the zero-extended divisor, subtract iff ≥, and emit that predicate as quotient bit.

Signed forms conditionally negate operands, divide magnitudes, negate quotient iff signs differ and remainder iff dividend negative; row fault predicates precede these outputs. | §4.2: "w (under ¬flag)" and the div fault predicates; §4.1 wrap/shift rules and signed MIN/−1 fault; §3.3 equal operand widths.

Lifted memory chooses the §7.2 mapped region in address order and scans its cells in increasing address order; captures use old addresses before exchanged counters. | §4.6: "for each cell i: under a == i"; §17 item 7: "one-hot address dispatch"; §3.7 C1–C5/R1–R5.
Row, oracle and structure | Compose these recipes in the printed §3.6 step order, §4.2 slot order, §3.7 activation order, §5.2 allocate/forward/commit/reverse/release order.

statements.text: The subject is a two-row oracle body `r = lift.add x a;` `lift.retval r`, widths x = target = fault = a = 2, with a preserved one-bit dirty bundle and an unused two-cell, two-bit `in` interface region; no inherited controls.
The **body** does not access memory; the interface cells remain part of D.
The reference payload is (1 + 2) mod 4 = 3: target 2 XOR 3 = 1 and fault 3 XOR 0 = 3.
The singleton declared domain is precisely `row.before`, within the full 11-bit D.
Four samples of singleton components draw no generator words and cover one of 2048 full tuples.
An identity implementation would agree with itself but MUST fail against `row`; using `wrong_row` also MUST fail.
At argument 1 the target is 2 XOR 2 = 0; at B = 1 the payload is zero and fault is 3 XOR 1 = 2.
A certificate for argument 2, B = 2 cannot be replayed as either of those invocations.
The printed rows illustrate the relation; bound closure/object hashes still have to be supplied in an actual certificate, not invented for this witness.

**Invocation contexts.** A subject denotes the set of invocations of the region `closure_hash`, with the given `variant` and `inherited_ controls`, in the root schedule `schedule_hash`: every invocation of the region in the root realisation's complete invocation tree — including invocations that no schedule entry names and defaults alone cover (§11) — with the classical arguments, budget, `epsilon_share`s and cleanup realisations resolved for it.

An invocation's **context key** is its concrete invocation chain (§11), outermost first, each element `{ "symbol", "point", "iteration" }` with every iteration index resolved and, for an element inside an oracle, `"step"` (1..B) and `"phase"` (`"fwd"` or `"rev"`) added; contexts are enumerated in increasing bytewise order of the JCS encodings of their keys (wildcard selectors play no part).
Every claim bound and every `error` entry (§12.3) is a **common upper bound over all contexts** of its key; the multiplicity composition of §12.3 is sound for that reason.
**Diamond-norm SDP** (Watrous, *Theory of Computing* 5 (2009), §4; the Hermiticity-preserving simplification).
Let Φ = Φ_real − Φ_ref be the difference of the subject's realised channel and the reference channel (both on the subject's interface, controls included), d_in = d_out = d the dimension.
The **Choi matrix** is J(Φ) = Σ_{i,j} |i⟩⟨j| ⊗ Φ(|i⟩⟨j|) (input factor first, output factor second, computational basis in allocation order, **unnormalised**).
The witness is a Hermitian Y of dimension d² and a decimal mu.

The checker accepts iff, with every matrix entry an interval and every test rigorous (an inconclusive test rejects): Y − J(Φ) ⪰ 0, Y + J(Φ) ⪰ 0, mu·I − Tr_out(Y) ⪰ 0 (partial trace over the output factor), and mu ≤ `bound`; then ‖Φ‖◇ ≤ mu (the dual of Watrous's SDP with Y₀ = Y₁ = Y; this is the diamond norm itself, not half of it). *(non-normative)* With this input-first Choi convention Tr_out traces the second factor, Tr[(ρ ⊗ I)Y] = Tr[ρ Tr_out(Y)]; a primal formulation that labels the input factor ρᵀ ranges over the same set of density matrices, so the bound is unchanged.
Encoding: `Y` is a row-major array of entries `[re_lo, re_ hi, im_lo, im_hi]` (decimal strings).

**Positivity test.** The checker proves each of the three matrices **positive definite** by an interval Cholesky (or Hermitian LDL†) factorisation in which the interval lower bound of every pivot is strictly positive, and rejects otherwise; no other test is admitted (nonnegative leading principal minors do not imply positive semidefiniteness: diag(0, −1)).

Producers make witnesses strictly feasible by replacing Y with Y + δI and mu with mu′ = mu + δ·(d + 1) for a small rational δ > 0 (any mu′ > mu + δ·d suffices): then Y ± J(Φ) ⪰ δI ≻ 0 and, since Tr_out(Y + δI) = Tr_out(Y) + δ·d·I, mu′·I − Tr_out(Y + δI) ⪰ δI ≻ 0; ‖Φ‖◇ ≤ mu′, which MUST be ≤ `bound`.
That recipe assumes an exactly feasible witness.
